Finite time blow up for a 1D model of 2D Boussinesq systemThanks: Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI 53706, USA; email: kchoi@math.wisc.eduThanks: Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI 53706, USA; email: kiselev@math.wisc.eduThanks: Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin, Madison, WI 53706, USA; email: yaoyao@math.wisc.edu

Kyudong Choi , Alexander Kiselev and Yao Yao
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

The 2D conservative Boussinesq system describes inviscid, incompressible, buoyant fluid flow in gravity field. The possibility of finite time blow up for solutions of this system is a classical problem of mathematical hydrodynamics. We consider a 1D model of 2D Boussinesq system motivated by a particular finite time blow up scenario. We prove that finite time blow up is possible for the solutions to the model system.

1. Introduction

The 2D Boussinesq system for vorticity of the fluid ω⁡(x,t)\omega(x,t) and density (or temperature) ρ⁡(x,t)\rho(x,t) is given by

(1) ∂tω+(u⋅∇)ω=∂x1ρ;∂tρ+(u⋅∇)ρ=0;\displaystyle\partial_{t}\omega+(u\cdot\nabla)\omega=\partial_{x_{1}}\rho;\,\,\,\,\,\,\partial_{t}\rho+(u\cdot\nabla)\rho=0;
u=∇⟂(−Δ)−1​ω,ω⁡(x,0)=ω0​(x),ρ⁡(x,0)=ρ0​(x).\displaystyle u=\nabla^{\perp}(-\Delta)^{-1}\omega,\,\,\,\omega(x,0)=\omega_{0}(x),\,\,\,\rho(x,0)=\rho_{0}(x).

The 2D Boussinesq system models motion of buoyant incompressible fluid that takes place in atmosphere, ocean, inside Earth or stars, and in every kitchen. Global regularity of solutions is known when classical dissipation is present in at least one of the equations [3], [9], or under a variety of more general conditions on dissipation (see e.g. [2] for more information). The regularity vs finite time blow up question for the inviscid 2D Boussinesq system (1) is a well known open problem that has appeared, for example, on the “eleven great problems of mathematical hydrodynamics” list proposed by Yudovich [17]. There is also an interesting connection between (1) and axi-symmetric three dimensional Euler equation: the equations are closely related and virtually identical away from the rotation axis (see e.g. [15], page 186).

There has been much numerical work on trying to find possible singular scenario for solutions of axi-symmetric 3D Euler equation with swirl or 2D Boussinesq system. Often, situations where strong growth of solutions has been observed were later determined to be regular by further numerical or analytic research. For numerical studies, see for example [16], [7], or a review [8]. Analytical tools for ruling out blow up scenario include nonlinearity depletion mechanisms discovered by Constantin, Fefferman and Majda [5], [6] and later extensions in [10], [11].

In a recent work [12], Tom Hou and Guo Luo suggested a new scenario for possible singularity formation in 3D Euler equation. In their scenario, the flow is axi-symmetric and confined in a rotating cylinder with no flow condition on the boundary. The numerically observed growth of vorticity happens at the boundary of the cylinder, away from rotation axis. So one can equivalently work with (1) set on a square DD (corresponding to a fixed angular variable in the 3D case). Motivated by [12], Kiselev and Sverak [14] considered a similar setting for the 2D Euler equation on a disk. The solutions of 2D Euler equation with smooth initial data are well known to be globally regular. However the work [14] constructs examples with double exponential growth of the vorticity gradient. This is known to be the fastest possible rate of growth, and [14] provides the first example where such growth happens. The growth in [14] also happens on the boundary, and their result confirms that the scenario of [12] is indeed an interesting candidate to consider for blow up in solutions of 3D Euler equation or 2D Boussinesq system.

Compared to the 2D Euler case, the 2D Boussinesq system presents significant new difficulties for analysis. There are nonlinear effects coming from the coupling in (1), and possible growth in vorticity makes solutions harder to control. A simplified one-dimensional model has been suggested in [12] and analyzed in [13]. It is given by

(2) ∂tω+u​∂xω=∂xρ;∂tρ+u​∂xρ=0;\displaystyle\partial_{t}\omega+u\partial_{x}\omega=\partial_{x}\rho;\,\,\,\partial_{t}\rho+u\partial_{x}\rho=0;
ux=H​ω,ω⁡(x,0)=ω0​(x),ρ⁡(x,0)=ρ0​(x)\displaystyle u_{x}=H\omega,\,\,\,\omega(x,0)=\omega_{0}(x),\,\,\,\rho(x,0)=\rho_{0}(x)

where the the initial data is periodic with period two, the density function is even, the vorticity is odd with respect to x=0x=0 and x=1,x=1, and H​ωH\omega denotes the periodic Hilbert transform of vorticity. Local well-posedness and a number of useful estimates have been proved in [13] for the system (2), and both numerical simulations as well as formal arguments suggesting blow up have been carried out. However a fully rigorous proof of finite time blow up is currently not available for the system (2).

Our goal in this paper is to analyze a related but further simplified system that is inspired by [14]. The system is set on an interval [0,1][0,1] with Dirichlet boundary conditions for ω\omega and ρ.\rho.

(3) {∂tρ⁡(t,x)+u⁡(t,x)​∂xρ⁡(t,x)=0,∂tω⁡(t,x)+u⁡(t,x)​∂xω⁡(t,x)=∂xρ⁡(t,x),u(t,x)=−xΩ(t,x),Ω(t,x)=∫x1ω⁡(t,y)ydy,ω(0,x)=ω0(x),ρ(0,x)=ρ0(x),ω0(0)=ω0(1)=ρ0(0)=ρ0(1)=0.\begin{cases}&\partial_{t}\rho(t,x)+u(t,x)\partial_{x}\rho(t,x)=0,\\[2.84544pt] &\partial_{t}\omega(t,x)+u(t,x)\partial_{x}\omega(t,x)=\partial_{x}\rho(t,x),\\[1.42271pt] &u(t,x)=-x\Omega(t,x),\quad\Omega(t,x)=\int_{x}^{1}\dfrac{\omega(t,y)}{y}dy,\\ &\omega(0,x)=\omega_{0}(x),\quad\rho(0,x)=\rho_{0}(x),\quad\omega_{0}(0)=\omega_{0}(1)=\rho_{0}(0)=\rho_{0}(1)=0.\\ \end{cases}

We choose to work with Dirichlet boundary conditions for both ω\omega and ρ,\rho, which is more natural than periodic setting for our version of the Biot-Savart law. The Biot-Savart law linking fluid velocity to vorticity is the main difference between (2) and (3). The law for the system (3) is simpler, even though closely related to the law for the system (2). This facilitates the analysis. Such simplified Biot-Savart law is motivated by the result proved in [14]. It is shown there that under certain conditions on the initial data ω0,\omega_{0}, the flow near the origin OO is hyperbolic for all times. Namely, apart from small exceptional sectors, the velocity uu near OO satisfies

(4) u1(x1,x2,t)=−4πx1∫Q⁡(x1,x2)y1​y2|y|4ω(y,t)dy1dy2+x1B1(x1,x2,t)\displaystyle u_{1}(x_{1},x_{2},t)=-\frac{4}{\pi}x_{1}\int_{Q(x_{1},x_{2})}\frac{y_{1}y_{2}}{|y|^{4}}\omega(y,t)\,dy_{1}dy_{2}+x_{1}B_{1}(x_{1},x_{2},t)
(5) u2​(x1,x2,t)=4π​x2​∫Q⁡(x1,x2)y1​y2|y|4​ω​(y,t)​d​y1​d​y2+x2​B2​(x1,x2,t),\displaystyle u_{2}(x_{1},x_{2},t)=\frac{4}{\pi}x_{2}\int_{Q(x_{1},x_{2})}\frac{y_{1}y_{2}}{|y|^{4}}\omega(y,t)\,dy_{1}dy_{2}+x_{2}B_{2}(x_{1},x_{2},t),

where x1,x2≥0,x_{1},x_{2}\geq 0, |B1,2​(x1,x2,t)|≤C⁡(γ)​‖ω‖L∞|B_{1,2}(x_{1},x_{2},t)|\leq C(\gamma)\|\omega\|_{L^{\infty}} and Q(x1,x2)={y|y∈D,x1≤y1,x2≤y2}.Q(x_{1},x_{2})=\{y|y\in D,\,\,\,x_{1}\leq y_{1},\,\,\,x_{2}\leq y_{2}\}. The first term on the right hand side of (4), (5) is the main term, and it is this term that is modeled by u(x,t)=−x∫x1ω(y,t)/ydyu(x,t)=-x\int_{x}^{1}\omega(y,t)/y\,dy in (3). Thus one can expect the system (3) to be a reasonable model of the true 2D Boussinesq dynamics as far as the hyperbolic flow formulas like (4), (5) remain valid, in particular all the time up to blow up if it happens. This is far from clear, even though the numerical simulations of Hou and Luo [12] seem to suggest that this might be the case.

In the first two sections below we will establish local well-posedness and conditional regularity results for the system (3), in particular proving an analog of the celebrated Beale-Kato-Majda criterion [1]. Then we will prove our main result

Theorem 1.1.

There exist ω0,ρ0∈C0∞​([0,1])\omega_{0},\rho_{0}\in C_{0}^{\infty}([0,1]) for which the solution of (3) blows up in finite time. In particular,

∫0T∗‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞​𝑑t→∞\int_{0}^{T^{*}}\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\,dt\rightarrow\infty

for some T∗<∞.T^{*}<\infty.

Roughly speaking, the blow-up proof is done by tracking the evolution of Ω⁡(x,t)\Omega(x,t) along a family of characteristics originating from a sequence of points x1≥x2≥…,x_{1}\geq x_{2}\geq\dots, where x∞:=limn→∞xn>0x_{\infty}:=\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}>0 satisfies ρ0​(x∞)>0\rho_{0}(x_{\infty})>0. By obtaining lower bound on Ω\Omega on this family of characteristics, we conclude that the characteristic originating from x∞x_{\infty} must touch the origin before some finite time TT, which implies that the classical solution has to break down at (or before) time TT.

The main new effect reflected in Theorem 1.1 is a rigorous understanding of the mechanism how coupling in 2D Boussinesq can in principle lead to blow up. The main simplifications the result utilizes are lack of two-dimensional geometry which makes certain monotonicity properties easier to control as well as reliance on the stable hyperbolic form of fluid velocity akin to [14]. These simplifications are clearly significant, but one has to take the first step.

Then the existence of a solution (ωϵ,ρϵ)∈C⁡([0,T],H0m×H0m+1)(\omega^{\epsilon},\rho^{\epsilon})\in C([0,T];H_{0}^{m}\times H_{0}^{m+1}) to (3) corresponding the mollified initial data (ω0ϵ,ρ0ϵ)(\omega^{\epsilon}_{0},\rho^{\epsilon}_{0}) follows the standard argument (e.g. see [15]).

We briefly sketch this argument here. First there exists a weak-∗* limit (ωϵ,ρϵ)∈L∞​(0,T,H0m×H0m+1),(\omega^{\epsilon},\rho^{\epsilon})\in L^{\infty}(0,T;H_{0}^{m}\times H_{0}^{m+1}), which follows from (8) by Banach-Alaoglu theorem. Then, by using (8) and (9), we can show strong convergence (ωnϵ,ρnϵ)→(ωϵ,ρϵ)(\omega_{n}^{\epsilon},\rho_{n}^{\epsilon})\rightarrow(\omega^{\epsilon},\rho^{\epsilon}) in C⁡([0,T],Hm−δ×Hm+1−δ)C([0,T];H^{m-\delta}\times H^{m+1-\delta}) for all real δ>0\delta>0. Recall that we assumed m≥2m\geq 2. Thus, from Sobolev’s inequality, all terms in (3) become continuous (pointwise). Moreover (6) converges pointwise to (3). It shows that (ωϵ,ρϵ)(\omega^{\epsilon},\rho^{\epsilon}) is a classical solution to (3). Since H−(m−δ)×H−(m+1−δ)H^{-(m-\delta)}\times H^{-(m+1-\delta)} is dense in H−m×H−(m+1)H^{-m}\times H^{-(m+1)}, our solution (ωϵ,ρϵ)(\omega^{\epsilon},\rho^{\epsilon}) is weakly continuous in time variable as a H0m×H0m+1H_{0}^{m}\times H_{0}^{m+1} valued function. Lastly, thanks to weak continuity in time and the estimate (7), we can show (ωϵ,ρϵ)∈C⁡([0,T],H0m×H0m+1)(\omega^{\epsilon},\rho^{\epsilon})\in C([0,T];H_{0}^{m}\times H_{0}^{m+1}) by showing that both ‖ωnϵ​(t)‖Hm\|\omega_{n}^{\epsilon}(t)\|_{H^{m}} and ‖ρnϵ​(t)‖Hm+1\|\rho_{n}^{\epsilon}(t)\|_{H^{m+1}} are continuous in time variable t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T]. (10) fϵ(t)≤1/((f0ϵ)−1/2−Ct)2, for 0≤t≤T.f^{\epsilon}(t)\leq 1/((f^{\epsilon}_{0})^{-1/2}-Ct)^{2},\quad\mbox{ for }0\leq t\leq T.

To find a solution for the original initial data (ω0,ρ0)(\omega_{0},\rho_{0}), recall that TT does not depend on ϵ\epsilon, the estimate (10) is uniform in ϵ>0\epsilon>0, and f0ϵf^{\epsilon}_{0} converges to f0f_{0} as ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0. Then we repeat the above procedure as ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0 in order to get a solution (ω,ρ)∈C⁡([0,T],H0m×H0m+1)(\omega,\rho)\in C([0,T];H_{0}^{m}\times H_{0}^{m+1}) to (3) corresponding to (ω0,ρ0)(\omega_{0},\rho_{0}) with the same estimate

(∥ω(t)∥Hm2+∥ρ(t)∥Hm+12+1)≤1/((f0)−1/2−Ct)2 for 0≤t≤T.\Big(\|\omega(t)\|^{2}_{H^{m}}+\|\rho(t)\|^{2}_{H^{m+1}}+1\Big)\leq 1/((f_{0})^{-1/2}-Ct)^{2}\quad\mbox{ for }0\leq t\leq T.

Its uniqueness in the space C⁡([0,T],H0m×H0m+1)C([0,T];H_{0}^{m}\times H_{0}^{m+1}) is easy to show (e.g. see [4]).

3. Beale-Kato-Majda type criteria

Proposition 3.1.

Let (ω,ρ)∈C⁡([0,T),H0m×H0m+1)(\omega,\rho)\in C([0,T);H^{m}_{0}\times H_{0}^{m+1}) be the unique solution provided by Proposition 2.2 for initial data (ω0,ρ0)∈H0m×H0m+1(\omega_{0},\rho_{0})\in H^{m}_{0}\times H^{m+1}_{0} with m≥2m\geq 2. Then for any finite T∗≤TT^{*}\leq T, the followings are equivalent:
(1). supt∈[0,T∗](‖ω⁡(t)‖Hm+‖ρ⁡(t)‖Hm+1)<∞\sup_{t\in[0,T^{*}]}\Big(\|\omega(t)\|_{H^{m}}+\|\rho(t)\|_{H^{m+1}}\Big)<\infty.
(2). ∫0T∗‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L∞​𝑑t<∞\int_{0}^{T^{*}}\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}dt<\infty.
(3). ∫0T∗‖ω⁡(t)‖L∞​𝑑t<∞\int_{0}^{T^{*}}\|\omega(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}dt<\infty.
(4). ∫0T∗‖∂xρ⁡(t)‖L∞​𝑑t<∞\int_{0}^{T^{*}}\|\partial_{x}\rho(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}dt<\infty.

Remark 3.1.

It is well known that for a full 2D inviscid Boussinesq system, either ∫0T∗‖∇u​(t)‖L∞​𝑑t<∞\int_{0}^{T^{*}}\|\nabla u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}dt<\infty or ∫0T∗‖∇ρ​(t)‖L∞​𝑑t<∞\int_{0}^{T^{*}}\|\nabla\rho(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}dt<\infty implies (1) (see e.g. [4], [2]). Whether (3) implies (1) for 2D inviscid Boussinesq system is an interesting open question.

Proof.

The implication (1)⇒(2),(3)(1)\Rightarrow(2),(3) and (4)(4) is obvious from Sobolev’s inequality.

The direction (2)⇒(1)(2)\Rightarrow(1) follows from a standard energy estimate. Indeed, if we denote M:=∫0T∗‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L∞​𝑑t<∞M:=\int_{0}^{T^{*}}\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}dt<\infty, then we get for any t∈[0,T∗]t\in[0,T^{*}],

Then straightforward estimates lead us to

‖ω′​(t)‖L2+‖ρ′′​(t)‖L2≤CM,T∗,‖ω0‖H1,‖ρ0‖H2and‖ω′​(t)‖L∞+‖ρ′′​(t)‖L∞≤CM,T∗,‖ω0‖W1,∞,‖ρ0‖W2,∞.\begin{split}&\|\omega^{\prime}(t)\|_{L^{2}}+\|\rho^{\prime\prime}(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq C_{M,T^{*},\|\omega_{0}\|_{H^{1}},\|\rho_{0}\|_{H^{2}}}\quad\mbox{and}\\ &\|\omega^{\prime}(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\rho^{\prime\prime}(t)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{M,T^{*},\|\omega_{0}\|_{W^{1,\infty}},\|\rho_{0}\|_{W^{2,\infty}}.}\\ \end{split}

where Wn,pW^{n,p} is the usual Sobolev space. We repeat this procedure until we get

‖ω(m)​(t)‖L2+‖ρ(m+1)​(t)‖L2≤CM,T∗,‖ω0‖Hm,‖ρ0‖Hm+1.\|\omega^{(m)}(t)\|_{L^{2}}+\|\rho^{(m+1)}(t)\|_{L^{2}}\leq C_{M,T^{*},\|\omega_{0}\|_{H^{m}},\|\rho_{0}\|_{H^{m+1}}}.

For (4)⇒\Rightarrow(3), we use the characteristic representation for ω\omega:

4. Finite-time blow up examples

Before we construct a finite-time blow up example, let us first state a lemma concerning the growth of Ω\Omega along the characteristics ϕt​(x)\phi_{t}(x).

Lemma 4.1.

Along the characteristic ϕt​(x)\phi_{t}(x), we have

(11) dd​t​Ω​(t,ϕt​(x))=∫ϕt​(x)1ω​(t,y)2y​𝑑y+∫ϕt​(x)1∂xρ⁡(t,y)y​𝑑y.\frac{d}{dt}\Omega(t,\phi_{t}(x))=\int_{\phi_{t}(x)}^{1}\frac{\omega(t,y)^{2}}{y}dy+\int_{\phi_{t}(x)}^{1}\frac{\partial_{x}\rho(t,y)}{y}dy.
Proof.

Note that

(12) dd​t​Ω​(t,ϕt​(x))=∂tΩ⁡(t,ϕt​(x))+u⁡(t,ϕt​(x))​∂xΩ⁡(t,ϕt​(x)).\begin{split}\frac{d}{dt}\Omega(t,\phi_{t}(x))&=\partial_{t}\Omega(t,\phi_{t}(x))+u(t,\phi_{t}(x))~\partial_{x}\Omega(t,\phi_{t}(x)).\end{split}

Let us compute ∂xΩ\partial_{x}\Omega and ∂tΩ\partial_{t}\Omega respectively. The definition of Ω\Omega directly gives that

(13) ∂xΩ⁡(t,x)=−ω⁡(t,x)x,\partial_{x}\Omega(t,x)=-\dfrac{\omega(t,x)}{x},

whereas ∂tΩ⁡(t,x)\partial_{t}\Omega(t,x) can be computed as follows:

(14) ∂tΩ⁡(t,x)=∫x1∂tω⁡(t,y)ydy=−∫x1u⁡(t,y)​∂xω⁡(t,y)ydy+∫x1∂xρ⁡(t,y)ydy=∫x1Ω⁡(t,y)​∂xω⁡(t,y)​𝑑y+∫x1∂xρ⁡(t,y)y​𝑑y=−Ω⁡(t,x)​ω​(t,x)+∫x1ω​(t,y)2y​dy+∫x1∂xρ⁡(t,y)y​dy.\begin{split}\partial_{t}\Omega(t,x)&=\int_{x}^{1}\frac{\partial_{t}\omega(t,y)}{y}dy=-\int_{x}^{1}\frac{u(t,y)\partial_{x}\omega(t,y)}{y}dy+\int_{x}^{1}\frac{\partial_{x}\rho(t,y)}{y}dy\\ &=\int_{x}^{1}{\Omega(t,y)\partial_{x}\omega(t,y)}dy+\int_{x}^{1}\frac{\partial_{x}\rho(t,y)}{y}dy\\ &=-\Omega(t,x)\omega(t,x)+\int_{x}^{1}\frac{\omega(t,y)^{2}}{y}dy+\int_{x}^{1}\frac{\partial_{x}\rho(t,y)}{y}dy.\end{split}

In order to obtain (11), it suffices to replace xx by ϕt​(x)\phi_{t}(x) in (13) and (14), and plug them into (12). ∎

We now prove the following Proposition from which, given Proposition 3.1, Theorem 1.1 follows.

Proposition 4.2.

There exist a pair of smooth functions ρ0\rho_{0} and ω0\omega_{0} supported in [14,34][\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4}], such that there is no global classical solution to (3) with initial data (ρ0,ω0)(\rho_{0},\omega_{0}).

Proof.

Step 1. We construct a pair of initial data (ρ0,ω0)(\rho_{0},\omega_{0}) as follows. Let ρ0\rho_{0} be smooth, nonnegative, supported in [14,34][\frac{1}{4},\frac{3}{4}], with max⁡ρ0=ρ0​(12)=2\max\rho_{0}=\rho_{0}(\frac{1}{2})=2, and ρ0​(13)=1\rho_{0}(\frac{1}{3})=1. Moreover, assume ρ0\rho_{0} is increasing in [14,12][\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2}], and decreasing in [12,34][\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{4}]. Let ω0\omega_{0} be smooth, nonnegative, supported in [14,12][\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2}], with ω0≡M\omega_{0}\equiv M in [0.3,0.45][0.3,0.45], where MM is a large constant to be determined later. Figure 1 gives a sketch of the initial data.

Towards a contradiction we assume that there is a global classical solution. Let us first make a few observations. Note that for all x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1), the characteristic ϕt​(x)\phi_{t}(x) must be well-defined for all time, and ρ\rho is conserved along ϕt​(x)\phi_{t}(x), i.e. ρ⁡(t,ϕt​(x))=ρ0​(x)\rho(t,\phi_{t}(x))=\rho_{0}(x). To see this, recall that by definition, ρ0\rho_{0} is decreasing in [12,1][\frac{1}{2},1]. If there is a global classical solution, then the characteristics do not cross, hence for all t≥0t\geq 0, we have ρx​(x,t)≤0\rho_{x}(x,t)\leq 0 in [ϕt​(1/2),1][\phi_{t}(1/2),1]. We then obtain (15) as a direct consequence, since the time derivative of ω\omega along the characteristics ϕt​(x)\phi_{t}(x) is equal to ρx\rho_{x}.

Moreover, we have that ϕt​(1/2)\phi_{t}(1/2) is increasing for all tt. Note that

dd​tϕt(1/2)=−ϕt(1/2)Ω(t,ϕt(1/2))=−ϕt(1/2)∫ϕt​(1/2)1ω⁡(y,t)ydy,\frac{d}{dt}\phi_{t}(1/2)=-\phi_{t}(1/2)\Omega(t,\phi_{t}(1/2))=-\phi_{t}(1/2)\int_{\phi_{t}(1/2)}^{1}\frac{\omega(y,t)}{y}dy,

which is always non-negative due to (15).

This would imply that the classical solution has to break down at (or before) time TT. To show this, the main idea is to consider a family of characteristics originating from a sequence of points {xn}\{x_{n}\}. Let x1=1/3x_{1}=1/3 (recall that we let OPENρ0​(13)=1)\rho_{0}(\frac{1}{3})=1). For n>1n>1, find xn∈[0,12]x_{n}\in[0,\frac{1}{2}], such that ρ0​(xn)=12+2−n\rho_{0}(x_{n})=\frac{1}{2}+2^{-n}. Observe that we have x1>x2>x3>⋯x_{1}>x_{2}>x_{3}>\cdots since ρ0\rho_{0} is increasing in [0,12][0,\frac{1}{2}]. Denote x∞:=limn→∞xnx_{\infty}:=\lim_{n\to\infty}x_{n}, and it follows that x∞>0x_{\infty}>0 and ρ⁡(x∞)=1/2\rho(x_{\infty})=1/2. The choice of {xn}\{x_{n}\} is illustrated in Figure 2.

Also, we choose MM large enough such that C0:=Ω⁡(0,x1)=∫1/31ω0​(y)y​𝑑y>20C_{0}:=\Omega(0,x_{1})=\int_{1/3}^{1}\frac{\omega_{0}(y)}{y}dy>20 (e.g. M=200M=200 should work). Note that at t=0t=0, Ω⁡(0,x)\Omega(0,x) is decreasing in xx due to the non-negativity of ω0\omega_{0}. This implies that at t=0t=0, we have Ω⁡(0,xn)>20\Omega(0,x_{n})>20 for all n≥1n\geq 1.

Let us denote ρn:=ρ0​(xn)\rho_{n}:=\rho_{0}(x_{n}), Φn​(t):=ϕt​(xn)\Phi_{n}(t):=\phi_{t}(x_{n}), Ωn​(t):=Ω⁡(t,Φn​(t))\Omega_{n}(t):=\Omega(t,\Phi_{n}(t)). Observe that dd​t​Φn​(t)=u⁡(t,Φn​(t))=−Φn​(t)​Ωn​(t)\frac{d}{dt}\Phi_{n}(t)=u(t,\Phi_{n}(t))=-\Phi_{n}(t)\Omega_{n}(t). Denoting ψn​(t):=−ln⁡Φn​(t)\psi_{n}(t):=-\ln\Phi_{n}(t) for n≥1n\geq 1, we get

For n≥2n\geq 2, using (16), we have
